author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book II.1, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil. But I who have seen the nature of the good that it is beautiful, and of the bad that it is ugly, and the nature of him who does wrong, that it is akin to me; not [only] of the same blood or seed, but that it participates in [the same] intelligence and [the same] portion of the divinity, I can neither be injured by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him.
morning_prompt: Name one person likely to test you today, and decide now to treat them as a kinsman.
evening_question: Who tested you today, and did you answer as a kinsman or as an opponent?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue §4, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: Man is a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman—a rope over an abyss. A dangerous crossing, a dangerous wayfaring, a dangerous looking-back, a dangerous trembling and halting. What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not a goal: what is lovable in man is that he is an OVER-GOING and a DOWN-GOING.
morning_prompt: Treat today as a crossing, not a destination: what are you becoming?
evening_question: Did you move toward who you want to be today, or stand still on the rope?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. I, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power. Within our power are opinion, aim, desire, aversion, and, in one word, whatever affairs are our own. Beyond our power are body, property, reputation, office, and, in one word, whatever are not properly our own affairs. Now the things within our power are by nature free, unrestricted, unhindered; but those beyond our power are weak, dependent, restricted, alien.
morning_prompt: Sort today's biggest worry into what is up to you and what is not; act only on the first.
evening_question: What did you spend energy on today that was never within your power?

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 2 (“The Old Buffoon”), trans. Constance Garnett (1912)
passage: Above all, don’t lie to yourself. The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others.
morning_prompt: Watch today for one small lie you tell yourself.
evening_question: What did you tell yourself today that was not quite true?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (“On Saving Time”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: Therefore, Lucilius, do as you write me that you are doing: hold every hour in your grasp. Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by. Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
morning_prompt: Pick today's one task and do it before anything you could postpone.
evening_question: Where did today's time actually go, and which hour would you take back?

author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: Either/Or, “Diapsalmata”, in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard, trans. Lee M. Hollander (1923)
passage: Let others complain that the times are wicked. I complain that they are paltry; for they are without passion. The thoughts of men are thin and frail like lace, and they themselves are feeble like girl lace-makers. The thoughts of their hearts are too puny to be sinful.
morning_prompt: Do one thing today with your whole heart instead of half of it.
evening_question: Where were you lukewarm today when something deserved passion?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book IV.3, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul, particularly when he has within him such thoughts that by looking into them he is immediately in perfect tranquillity; and I affirm that tranquillity is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind. Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself; and let thy principles be brief and fundamental, which, as soon as thou shalt recur to them, will be sufficient to cleanse the soul completely, and to send thee back free from all discontent with the things to which thou returnest.
morning_prompt: Choose one brief principle you can return to whenever the day gets loud.
evening_question: When did you most need an inner retreat today, and did you take it?

author: Jean-Paul Sartre
source: Paraphrase of Existentialism Is a Humanism (lecture, Paris, 1945; published 1946)
passage: A paper-knife is designed before it is made: its purpose comes first. Sartre argues that people are the reverse. We exist first, turn up in the world, and only afterwards define ourselves by what we do. There is no blueprint of human nature you were built to match; you are the sum of your choices and acts, and you are still making yourself.
morning_prompt: Choose one act today that defines who you are, rather than who you were told to be.
evening_question: If you were only the sum of what you did today, who would you be?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. V, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things. Thus death is nothing terrible, else it would have appeared so to Socrates. But the terror consists in our notion of death, that it is terrible. When, therefore, we are hindered or disturbed, or grieved, let us never impute it to others, but to ourselves—that is, to our own views. It is the action of an uninstructed person to reproach others for his own misfortunes; of one entering upon instruction, to reproach himself; and one perfectly instructed, to reproach neither others nor himself.
morning_prompt: When something upsets you today, name the judgment you added to the event.
evening_question: What upset you today, and what view of it did the upsetting?

author: Albert Camus
source: Paraphrase of The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), final chapter, “The Myth of Sisyphus”
passage: The gods condemned Sisyphus to push a rock up a hill forever, only to watch it roll back down. Camus dwells on the walk back down, when Sisyphus knows exactly how hopeless his task is and goes back to it anyway. Seeing his fate clearly and refusing to be crushed by it makes him greater than it. The struggle itself, Camus concludes, can be enough to fill a heart, and he asks us to picture Sisyphus as happy.
morning_prompt: Pick today's most repetitive task and do it with full attention instead of resentment.
evening_question: Which rock did you push today, and could you find any happiness in pushing it?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 2 (“On Discursiveness in Reading”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: Each day acquire something that will fortify you against poverty, against death, indeed against other misfortunes as well; and after you have run over many thoughts, select one to be thoroughly digested that day.
morning_prompt: Choose one idea from this passage to carry with you all day.
evening_question: What single thought from today is worth keeping, and why that one?

author: Simone de Beauvoir
source: Paraphrase of The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947)
passage: Beauvoir argues that freedom is never purely private. My projects only make sense in a world shared with other free people, so wanting to be free myself means wanting others to be free as well. Oppressing someone, or simply treating them as an obstacle or a tool, contradicts the very freedom I claim for myself.
morning_prompt: Look for one way to widen someone else's freedom today.
evening_question: Did anything you did today make someone else's choices smaller?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book V.1, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,--I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world? Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?--But this is more pleasant.--Dost thou exist then to take thy pleasure, and not at all for action or exertion? Dost thou not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees working together to put in order their several parts of the universe? And art thou unwilling to do the work of a human being, and dost thou not make haste to do that which, is according to thy nature?
morning_prompt: Name the work you exist to do today, and start it before you feel ready.
evening_question: Did you do the work of a human being today, or mostly keep yourself warm?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue §5, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: I tell you: one must still have chaos in one, to give birth to a dancing star. I tell you: ye have still chaos in you.
morning_prompt: Let something unfinished or messy in you be material for making something today.
evening_question: What chaos in you today could become a dancing star?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. VIII, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.
morning_prompt: Expect at least one thing to go differently than planned, and decide to want it anyway.
evening_question: What happened today that you fought, and what would accepting it have looked like?

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4 (“A Lady of Little Faith”), trans. Constance Garnett (1912)
passage: …love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Love in dreams is greedy for immediate action, rapidly performed and in the sight of all. Men will even give their lives if only the ordeal does not last long but is soon over, with all looking on and applauding as though on the stage. But active love is labor and fortitude, and for some people too, perhaps, a complete science.
morning_prompt: Do one unglamorous, patient act of love today that nobody will applaud.
evening_question: Was your love today in action or only in dreams?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 5 (“On the Philosopher’s Mean”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: The first thing which philosophy undertakes to give is fellow-feeling with all men; in other words, sympathy and sociability. We part company with our promise if we are unlike other men.
morning_prompt: Let your principles show today as kindness, not as distance from people.
evening_question: Did anything you believe today make you warmer to others, or colder?

author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: Fear and Trembling, “Preliminary Expectoration”, in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard, trans. Lee M. Hollander (1923)
passage: He takes pleasure in all things, is interested in everything, and perseveres in whatever he does with the zest characteristic of persons wholly given to worldly things. He attends to his business, and when one sees him one might think he was a clerk who had lost his soul in doing double bookkeeping, he is so exact.
morning_prompt: Bring full attention to one ordinary errand today.
evening_question: What ordinary thing did you take real pleasure in today?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book IV.7, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
morning_prompt: Notice the moment you think “I have been harmed”, and test whether it is true.
evening_question: What felt like harm today, and was any real harm done to your character?

author: Jean-Paul Sartre
source: Paraphrase of Existentialism Is a Humanism (lecture, Paris, 1945; published 1946)
passage: Sartre says that when you choose how to live, you are not choosing only for yourself. Each choice quietly answers the question of what a person ought to be, as if you were setting an example for everyone. That is the source of anguish: no rulebook or authority can take the weight from you, and even deciding whose advice to ask is already your choice. His example is a student torn between caring for his mother and joining the Free French; no moral system could decide it for him.
morning_prompt: Before one decision today, ask: would I want everyone to choose this way?
evening_question: Which choice did you make today as if it were an example for everyone?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. XI, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: Never say of anything, “I have lost it,” but, “I have restored it.” Has your child died? It is restored. Has your wife died? She is restored. Has your estate been taken away? That likewise is restored. “But it was a bad man who took it.” What is it to you by whose hands he who gave it has demanded it again? While he permits you to possess it, hold it as something not your own, as do travelers at an inn.
morning_prompt: Hold one thing you love today as a traveler holds a room at an inn.
evening_question: What are you holding as if it were permanently yours?

author: Albert Camus
source: Paraphrase of The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), “An Absurd Reasoning”
passage: Camus begins by saying there is only one truly serious philosophical question: whether life is worth living. The absurd is the collision between our hunger for meaning and a world that does not answer. His response is neither despair nor a leap into comforting certainty, but to live with that tension wide awake, with revolt, freedom and passion.
morning_prompt: Live one hour today fully awake, without distraction from the question of what it is for.
evening_question: When did you feel most alive today, and was it because you were paying attention?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 7 (“On Crowds”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.
morning_prompt: Spend time today with someone who makes you better, or someone you can help.
evening_question: Who did you spend today with, and did they make you better or worse?

author: Simone de Beauvoir
source: Paraphrase of The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), Part II
passage: Beauvoir describes the ‘serious man’, who hands his freedom over to ready-made values such as a cause, a career or a nation, and then treats them as absolute so he never has to choose. She argues that values are not given in advance; they exist only because free people keep taking them up, and we stay responsible for them.
morning_prompt: Name one value you follow by default and decide whether you actually choose it.
evening_question: Where did you hide behind a rule or role today instead of choosing?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book X.16, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
morning_prompt: Pick one virtue to practice today instead of thinking about it.
evening_question: Where did you talk about being good today instead of being it?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part I, “The Three Metamorphoses”, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: Innocence is the child, and forgetfulness, a new beginning, a game, a self-rolling wheel, a first movement, a holy Yea. Aye, for the game of creating, my brethren, there is needed a holy Yea unto life: ITS OWN will, willeth now the spirit; HIS OWN world winneth the world’s outcast.
morning_prompt: Approach one thing today as a beginner, with a holy yes instead of a grudge.
evening_question: What did you start fresh today, and what are you still carrying like a camel?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. XVII, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: Remember that you are an actor in a drama of such sort as the Author chooses—if short, then in a short one; if long, then in a long one. If it be his pleasure that you should enact a poor man, or a cripple, or a ruler, or a private citizen, see that you act it well. For this is your business—to act well the given part, but to choose it belongs to another.
morning_prompt: Name the role today has handed you, and play it well rather than wishing for another.
evening_question: Which part did you play today, and did you act it well?

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 3 (“Conversations and Exhortations of Father Zossima”), trans. Constance Garnett (1912)
passage: Love all God’s creation, the whole and every grain of sand in it. Love every leaf, every ray of God’s light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things. Once you perceive it, you will begin to comprehend it better every day. And you will come at last to love the whole world with an all-embracing love.
morning_prompt: Notice and appreciate one small living thing today: a leaf, an animal, a person.
evening_question: What did you love today that you would normally walk past?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 (“On Groundless Fears”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. I am not speaking with you in the Stoic strain but in my milder style. For it is our Stoic fashion to speak of all those things, which provoke cries and groans, as unimportant and beneath notice; but you and I must drop such great-sounding words, although, Heaven knows, they are true enough. What I advise you to do is, not to be unhappy before the crisis comes; since it may be that the dangers before which you paled as if they were threatening you, will never come upon you; they certainly have not yet come.
morning_prompt: Name one fear for today and ask whether it has actually arrived.
evening_question: Which of today's worries happened, and which only lived in your imagination?

author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: Either/Or, “Diapsalmata”, in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard, trans. Lee M. Hollander (1923)
passage: Of all ridiculous things the most ridiculous seems to me, to be busy--to be a man who is brisk about his food and his work. Therefore, whenever I see a fly settling, in the decisive moment, on the nose of such a person of affairs; or if he is spattered with mud from a carriage which drives past him in still greater haste; or the drawbridge opens up before him; or a tile falls down and knocks him dead, then I laugh heartily. And who, indeed, could help laughing? What, I wonder, do these busy folks get done? Are they not to be classed with the woman who in her confusion about the house being on fire carried out the fire-tongs? What things of greater account, do you suppose, will they rescue from life's great conflagration?
morning_prompt: Before rushing today, ask what you would actually rescue from the fire.
evening_question: What did your busyness today actually accomplish?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book IV.17, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
morning_prompt: Do one good thing today that you have been saving for later.
evening_question: If today had been your last, what would you wish you had done differently?

author: Jean-Paul Sartre
source: Paraphrase of Being and Nothingness (1943), Part One, ch. 2, “Bad Faith”
passage: Sartre describes a café waiter whose every movement is a little too precise, too eager, too quick, as though he were playing at being a waiter. Bad faith is this kind of self-deception: treating yourself as a fixed thing (“that's just who I am”, “I had no choice”) to escape the freedom and responsibility you actually have.
morning_prompt: Catch yourself saying “I had no choice” today, and look for the choice.
evening_question: Where did you play a role today to avoid owning a decision?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. XX, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: Remember that it is not he who gives abuse or blows, who affronts, but the view we take of these things as insulting. When, therefore, anyone provokes you, be assured that it is your own opinion which provokes you. Try, therefore, in the first place, not to be bewildered by appearances. For if you once gain time and respite, you will more easily command yourself.
morning_prompt: When provoked today, buy yourself a pause before you answer.
evening_question: What provoked you today, and was it the act or your opinion of it?

author: Albert Camus
source: Paraphrase of The Plague (1947), Part II
passage: In Camus's novel, Dr. Rieux keeps fighting an epidemic he cannot defeat. He has no grand theory of heroism; for him it is a matter of common decency, and decency simply means doing his job. Camus's point is that ordinary work done well, alongside others, is how people resist suffering.
morning_prompt: Do your job today as an act of decency toward the people it serves.
evening_question: Where did ordinary decency matter today?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 16 (“On Philosophy, the Guide of Life”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: Philosophy is no trick to catch the public; it is not devised for show. It is a matter, not of words, but of facts. It is not pursued in order that the day may yield some amusement before it is spent, or that our leisure may be relieved of a tedium that irks us. It moulds and constructs the soul; it orders our life, guides our conduct, shows us what we should do and what we should leave undone; it sits at the helm and directs our course as we waver amid uncertainties. Without it, no one can live fearlessly or in peace of mind.
morning_prompt: Let one decision today be guided by a principle rather than a mood.
evening_question: Where did philosophy actually steer your conduct today?

author: Simone de Beauvoir
source: Paraphrase of Pyrrhus and Cineas (1944)
passage: King Pyrrhus lays out his plans: conquer Greece, then Africa, then the world, and then rest. His adviser Cineas asks why he does not simply rest now. Beauvoir's answer is that no final resting point could make a life meaningful. We are always going beyond where we are, and meaning lives in the projects themselves and in how they open onto other people.
morning_prompt: Choose one project today for its own sake, not for the rest it promises later.
evening_question: What did you do today that was worth doing even if nothing came after it?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book V.20, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: Now it is true that these may impede my action, but they are no impediments to my affects and disposition, which have the power of acting conditionally and changing: for the mind converts and changes every hindrance to its activity into an aid; and so that which is a hindrance is made a furtherance to an act; and that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.
morning_prompt: Expect an obstacle today and look for how it can become part of the way.
evening_question: What blocked you today, and how could it have helped you instead?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part I, “Reading and Writing”, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: Of all that is written, I love only what a person hath written with his blood. Write with blood, and thou wilt find that blood is spirit.
morning_prompt: Write, say or make one thing today that you actually mean.
evening_question: What did you produce today that came from your own blood?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. XLIII, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: Everything has two handles: one by which it may be borne, another by which it cannot. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold on the affair by the handle of his injustice, for by that it cannot be borne, but rather by the opposite—that he is your brother, that he was brought up with you; and thus you will lay hold on it as it is to be borne.
morning_prompt: When someone wrongs you today, look for the handle by which it can be carried.
evening_question: Which handle did you grab today, the one that can be borne or the one that cannot?

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 1, Biographical Notes (a), “Father Zossima’s Brother”, trans. Constance Garnett (1912)
passage: “Mother, darling,” he would say, “there must be servants and masters, but if so I will be the servant of my servants, the same as they are to me. And another thing, mother, every one of us has sinned against all men, and I more than any.”
morning_prompt: Take responsibility today for something that is not strictly your fault.
evening_question: Where did you blame others today when you could have owned your part?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 18 (“On Festivals and Fasting”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: Set aside a certain number of days, during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, with coarse and rough dress, saying to yourself the while: “Is this the condition that I feared?”
morning_prompt: Go without one comfort today and notice what it is actually like.
evening_question: What did you do without today, and was it the condition you feared?

author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: Either/Or, “Diapsalmata”, in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard, trans. Lee M. Hollander (1923)
passage: When I was very young I forgot in the Trophonian cave how to laugh; but when I grew older and opened my eyes and contemplated the real world, I had to laugh, and have not ceased laughing, ever since. I beheld that the meaning of life was to make a living; its goal, to become Chief Justice; that the delights of love consisted in marrying a woman with ample means; that it was the blessedness of friendship to help one another in financial difficulties; that wisdom was what most people supposed it to be; that it showed enthusiasm to make a speech, and courage, to risk being fined 10 dollars; that it was cordiality to say "may it agree with you" after a repast; that it showed piety to partake of the communion once a year. I saw that and laughed.
morning_prompt: Notice one thing you chase today only because everyone else does.
evening_question: Which of today's goals would make Kierkegaard laugh?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book IV.49, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it. Unhappy am I because this has happened to me? Not so, but happy am I, though this has happened to me, because I continue free from pain, neither crushed by the present nor fearing the future.
morning_prompt: Decide in advance how you will stand firm when today's waves break.
evening_question: What broke against you today, and did you stay standing?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part I, “The Way of the Creating One”, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: Ready must thou be to burn thyself in thine own flame; how couldst thou become new if thou have not first become ashes!
morning_prompt: Let go of one old version of yourself today to make room for a new one.
evening_question: What in you needs to burn so something new can grow?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. XLVI, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: Never proclaim yourself a philosopher, nor make much talk among the ignorant about your principles, but show them by actions. Thus, at an entertainment, do not discourse how people ought to eat, but eat as you ought.
morning_prompt: Let your principles show in what you do today, without announcing them.
evening_question: Where did you explain your principles today instead of living them?

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Notes from Underground, Part I, ch. 7, trans. Constance Garnett (1918)
passage: …man everywhere and at all times, whoever he may be, has preferred to act as he chose and not in the least as his reason and advantage dictated. And one may choose what is contrary to one’s own interests, and sometimes one positively ought (that is my idea). One’s own free unfettered choice, one’s own caprice, however wild it may be, one’s own fancy worked up at times to frenzy—is that very “most advantageous advantage” which we have overlooked, which comes under no classification and against which all systems and theories are continually being shattered to atoms.
morning_prompt: Notice one choice today that you make freely, against what is merely advantageous.
evening_question: Did you act today from your own choice, or only from calculated advantage?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 28 (“On Travel as a Cure for Discontent”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: Socrates made the same remark to one who complained; he said: “Why do you wonder that globe-trotting does not help you, seeing that you always take yourself with you? The reason which set you wandering is ever at your heels.” What pleasure is there in seeing new lands? Or in surveying cities and spots of interest? All your bustle is useless. Do you ask why such flight does not help you? It is because you flee along with yourself.
morning_prompt: Instead of changing your surroundings today, change one thing in yourself.
evening_question: What were you trying to escape today that you carried with you anyway?

author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: The Present Moment, No. I, 1, “By Way of Introduction”, in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard, trans. Lee M. Hollander (1923)
passage: …true seriousness appears only when a man fully equal to his task is forced, against his will, to undertake it--against his will, but fully equal to the task.
morning_prompt: Take on one task today that you would rather avoid but are equal to.
evening_question: What did you take seriously today precisely because you did not want to?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book VIII.47, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now. But if anything in thy own disposition gives thee pain, who hinders thee from correcting thy opinion? And even if thou art pained because thou art not doing some particular thing which seems to thee to be right, why dost thou not rather act than complain?
morning_prompt: Turn one complaint today into one action.
evening_question: What pained you today, and was it the thing or your judgment of it?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part I, “Voluntary Death”, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: Many die too late, and some die too early. Yet strange soundeth the precept: “Die at the right time!” Die at the right time: so teacheth Zarathustra. To be sure, he who never liveth at the right time, how could he ever die at the right time?
morning_prompt: Live today at the right time: do the thing whose moment is now.
evening_question: Did you live today, or only wait for life to start?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. L, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: This instant, then, think yourself worthy of living as a man grown up and a proficient. Let whatever appears to be the best be to you an inviolable law. And if any instance of pain or pleasure, glory or disgrace, be set before you, remember that now is the combat, now the Olympiad comes on, nor can it be put off; and that by one failure and defeat honor may be lost or—won.
morning_prompt: Stop postponing one improvement you already know you need; begin it now.
evening_question: What did you put off today that you could have begun?

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 3 (“Conversations and Exhortations of Father Zossima”), trans. Constance Garnett (1912)
passage: Fathers and teachers, I ponder, “What is hell?” I maintain that it is the suffering of being unable to love.
morning_prompt: Look for one person today you find hard to love, and practise anyway.
evening_question: Where were you unable to love today, and what got in the way?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 47 (“On Master and Slave”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: Treat your inferiors as you would be treated by your betters. And as often as you reflect how much power you have over a slave, remember that your master has just as much power over you.
morning_prompt: Treat everyone with less power than you today the way you want to be treated by those with more.
evening_question: How did you treat the people who could do nothing for you today?

author: Søren Kierkegaard
source: Preparation for a Christian Life, “Christianity as the Absolute; Contemporaneousness with Christ”, in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard, trans. Lee M. Hollander (1923)
passage: That which is past is not a reality--for me, but only my time is. That which you are contemporaneous with, that is reality--for you.
morning_prompt: Treat today, not yesterday or someday, as the only time that is real for you.
evening_question: Did you live in your own time today, or in the past and the future?

author: Marcus Aurelius
source: Meditations, Book VI.30, trans. George Long (1862)
passage: Take care that thou art not made into a Caesar, that thou art not dyed with this dye; for such things happen. Keep thyself then simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, strenuous in all proper acts. Strive to continue to be such as philosophy wished to make thee.
morning_prompt: Pick one quality from this list to guard today against status or comfort.
evening_question: Where did success or power dye you a little today?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part I, “The Bestowing Virtue” §3, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: Ye had not yet sought yourselves: then did ye find me. So do all believers; therefore all belief is of so little account. Now do I bid you lose me and find yourselves; and only when ye have all denied me, will I return unto you.
morning_prompt: Question one idea you hold only because someone you admire holds it.
evening_question: Whose voice were you following today instead of your own?

author: Epictetus
source: Enchiridion, ch. IV, trans. Thomas Wentworth Higginson (1865)
passage: When you set about any action, remind yourself of what nature the action is. If you are going to bathe, represent to yourself the incidents usual in the bath—some persons pouring out, others pushing in, others scolding, others pilfering. And thus you will more safely go about this action if you say to yourself, “I will now go to bathe and keep my own will in harmony with nature.”
morning_prompt: Before your next task, picture what usually goes wrong and how you want to meet it.
evening_question: Which irritation today could you have predicted, and did predicting it help?

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: The Brothers Karamazov, Epilogue, ch. 3 (“Ilusha’s Funeral. The Speech at the Stone”), trans. Constance Garnett (1912)
passage: You must know that there is nothing higher and stronger and more wholesome and good for life in the future than some good memory, especially a memory of childhood, of home. People talk to you a great deal about your education, but some good, sacred memory, preserved from childhood, is perhaps the best education. If a man carries many such memories with him into life, he is safe to the end of his days, and if one has only one good memory left in one’s heart, even that may sometime be the means of saving us.
morning_prompt: Create one good memory today for yourself or someone else.
evening_question: What good memory from today would you want to carry for years?

author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 61 (“On Meeting Death Cheerfully”), trans. Richard M. Gummere (1917)
passage: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life. I do not indeed snatch it up as if it were my last; I do regard it, however, as if it might even be my last.
morning_prompt: Live today as if it were a complete life on its own.
evening_question: If today were the whole of your life, would it be enough?

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part III, “The Vision and the Enigma” §1, trans. Thomas Common (1909)
passage: Courage, however, is the best slayer, courage which attacketh: it slayeth even death itself; for it saith: “WAS THAT life? Well! Once more!”
morning_prompt: Face one thing today with the courage that says “Once more!”
evening_question: If you had to live today again, exactly as it was, would you say yes?
